1.d4 e6 2.c4.background: The most common reply to 1...e6, keeping the game in Queen's Pawn territory. Howard Staunton played 1...e6 five times in his 1843 match series against Saint-Amant, the strongest French player of the time, and each game transposed into a Queen's Gambit Declined with 2.c4 d5.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight and controls e4 while committing to nothing in the centre, so every set-up stays available and White decides the direction. The cost is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn until Black frees it.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Occupies the centre at once and heads for a Queen's Gambit Declined. The structure is solid, with natural development and castling to follow, but a little passive: the c8-bishop stays shut in behind the e6-pawn until Black frees it, and White keeps the initiative with pressure on d5.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+.name: Keres Defence
1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+.background: Named after the Estonian grandmaster Paul Keres and also called the Kangaroo Defence. The check was known from the 1840s, and Henry Thomas Buckle played it against Johann Löwenthal in the fourth game of their match in London in 1851; the standard reply today, 3.Bd2, was recommended by Howard Staunton.
1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+.strategy: Develops the bishop with check before Black commits the g8-knight, which keeps many set-ups open. White has several ways to answer, and the game often transposes into a better-known system. The cost is that the bishop may be exchanged or chased, so the move works best when Black is happy to reach one of those systems.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5.name: Dutch Defence
1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5.background: Elias Stein recommended the Dutch as the best reply to 1.d4 in his 1789 book, and both Botvinnik and Bronstein played it in their 1951 World Championship match. The English grandmaster Simon Williams often plays 1.d4 e6 as a way of reaching the Dutch while avoiding the Staunton Gambit (1.d4 f5 2.e4).
1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5.strategy: Stakes a claim to e4 and aims for kingside attacking chances, usually with a knight on f6 and a solid pawn set-up behind the f-pawn. The price is a loosened kingside, especially the e8-h5 diagonal, and a weakened e5 square.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop to its usual square in the Queen's Gambit Declined, with central development to follow. It gives up the active ...Bb4 and lets White take space in the centre at once, which the main replies prevent. Sound, but they reach the same structures without the concession.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4 and lets White build a broad centre, which Black then undermines instead of occupying it. A fair practical choice, but Black must play accurately against White's space.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 for a solid structure with the c-pawn behind the d-pawn. It commits the c-pawn before White shows a plan and lets White take space in the centre, so it is not recommended over the more flexible main replies.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and leaves the choice of structure to White: if White pushes 3.d5, the exchanges that follow give Black a queenside pawn majority, while exchanging on c5 releases the tension. Sound, but after 3.d5 Black has to accept White's extra space in the centre in return for queenside play.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and a fianchetto set-up that lets White build a centre, then aims to undermine it with pawn breaks. Sound but slow: the e6-pawn already shuts in the c8-bishop, and White gets a broad centre before Black's knight can challenge it.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and eyes d4 and e5, but blocks the c-pawn. 3.d5 gains space with a tempo on the knight, which can answer by going to e5 and stays sound, though White keeps the more comfortable game.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Aims for b4, or for c7 once the c-pawn has moved, but a knight on the rim does little for the centre and costs time. White takes space or develops while the knight is still looking for a square.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Qe7.strategy: Puts the queen on e7, where it blocks the f8-bishop's only open diagonal and does little for d5 or e4. White takes the centre or develops at leisure, and Black's queen is in the way of its own pieces.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Qf6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight and leaves the queen open to e4-e5 with gain of time. White simply develops and builds a centre.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Qh4.strategy: The queen comes out early and is attacked at once by 3.Nf3, which also guards d4, or by 3.g3, so White develops with tempo. Black has no pieces out to support it and loses time retreating.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bd6.strategy: Puts the bishop on d6, where it blocks the d-pawn and can be hit by c4-c5, e4-e5 or Nc3-b5. Nothing is prepared in the centre, and White takes space while the bishop looks for a better post.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 or g4 but runs into 3.Bxh6 gxh6, which wrecks the kingside pawns for good. A knight on the rim also does nothing for the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Ne7.strategy: Heads for f5 or g6 but blocks the f8-bishop, which can only come out after the knight moves on or a pawn move prepares a fianchetto. White builds a centre at leisure while the knight and bishop get in each other's way.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from White's pieces and prepares ...b5 against the c4-pawn, but spends a tempo on the wing before the centre is settled. Sound, since White has no way to punish it, yet the pieces stay at home while White develops.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Prepares ...Bb4+ with the pawn supporting the bishop, an idea from the Bogo-Indian, but it spends a tempo on the wing and weakens b5. White develops or takes the centre first.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for queenside pressure, but with White's pawn still on d4 and no black piece developed. After 3.cxb5 White is a clean pawn up, and Black's follow-up brings too little for it.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 d6.strategy: A slow, passive move that rules out the Queen's Gambit set-ups with ...d5. White takes the centre at leisure, and the e6-pawn keeps the c8-bishop cramped.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight and weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal while doing little for the centre. White takes space or develops, and Black's kingside pieces have no good squares.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Weakens the kingside and the dark squares for nothing. Only the queen guards the pawn against the c1-bishop, so after Nf3 Black must either support it or push on, which loosens the position further.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Stops Bg5, which would attack the queen, so the g8-knight can come out without a pin. It spends a tempo on a rim pawn and does nothing for the centre. Sound, since nothing punishes it, but White simply takes space.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook pawn that does nothing for the centre or development and gives up ...h6 as a way to keep a bishop off g5. White develops and takes the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 e5.name: Horwitz Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.d4 e6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for activity: 3.dxe5 wins a pawn, and Black has spent two moves on the e-pawn. Compensation must come from quick development, which is hard because White can keep the extra pawn with natural developing moves and meets any check easily.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Qg5.strategy: Loses the queen to 3.Bxg5: the c1-bishop's diagonal is open because the d-pawn has left d2, and the queen steps onto a square the bishop attacks.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and blocks the f8-bishop and the queen's d8-h4 diagonal. 3.Bg5+ checks at once along the open c1-h6 diagonal, and Black has to block or move the king again.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bc5.strategy: Loses a piece: the d4-pawn attacks c5 and nothing guards the bishop, so 3.dxc5 wins it for free.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Ba3.strategy: Loses the bishop: 3.Nxa3 or 3.bxa3 simply takes it, and Black has no compensation for the piece.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+ 3.Nc3.name: Kangaroo Defence: Keres Defence, Transpositional Variation
1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+ 3.Nc3.strategy: Blocks the check with the knight, which is then pinned against the king. That invites Black to double White's pawns or keep the pin and fight for e4. Playable, but the usual way to answer the check keeps the pawn structure intact.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+ 3.Bd2.strategy: The standard answer to the check: the bishop blocks it and itself attacks Black's bishop, so no pawns are doubled and both knights keep their best squares. White keeps the pawns on c4 and d4 and a small space edge, and can build a broad centre if Black declines to trade.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+ 3.Nd2.strategy: Blocks the check with the queen's knight, which is then pinned against the king, but keeps White's pawns intact. The knight shuts in the c1-bishop, so development is awkward: White gets a solid but slightly passive game, playable rather than ambitious.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5.strategy: Claims space with a pawn on d5 that cramps Black. If Black trades it, White gets a central pawn majority against Black's queenside one: a sharp, unbalanced game where White plays in the centre and Black on the queenside.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends d4 with a developing move and avoids committing the centre. If Black trades on d4, White recaptures with the knight and keeps a lead in development and a space edge on the queenside, with a flexible game ahead.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps the choice of centre open, but leaves d4 to its fate: if Black takes it, White can only recapture with the queen, and ...Nc6 attacks it at once with a developing move. A sound but unambitious game, without the space gain of pushing the d-pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for White's advanced pawn, so Black gets a half-open e-file and, after White recaptures with the c-pawn, a queenside pawn majority. Black gives up space in return for counterplay on the wing.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it eyes e4 and d5, and heads for the Benoni structure: Black will trade the e-pawn for White's d-pawn and play on the queenside majority. Black accepts a sharp game in which White's central space and kingside play must be met accurately.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5.strategy: Locks the centre with pawns on c5 and e5 against White's d5. Solid, but Black is cramped: the c8-bishop is shut in behind the d7-pawn, and counterplay waits for slow breaks on the wings while White builds up at leisure.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5.strategy: Recaptures towards the centre. The pawn on d5 cramps Black, and White has a central majority against Black's queenside one. A sharp, unbalanced game: White plays in the centre and on the kingside, Black on the queenside.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which keeps material level but brings it out early: Black develops with tempo against it, and White ends up behind in development. The pawn on c5 stays safe, defended by the bishop. Playable, but it hands Black the initiative in development.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops, but leaves the pawn on c4 attacked: Black takes it, and even if the queen wins a pawn back with check on a4, White has given two pawns for one. A natural-looking move that simply drops a pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 d6.strategy: Supports the c5 pawn and fixes the structure instead of trying to win the d5 pawn at once. It also opens the diagonal of the bishop on c8 and gives Black a solid base for the queenside majority.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight, attacks d5 and eyes e4, aiming for play against the queenside. Sound, but White defends with Nc3 and builds a broad centre that the knight alone cannot hold back, so Black has to play accurately to keep the balance.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 Bd6.strategy: Guards c5 and develops, but occupies d6, the square the d-pawn needs to fix the structure, and the bishop becomes a target for e4-e5. White takes a broad centre while Black's pieces get in each other's way.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 d6 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the knight, protects the pawn on d5 and prepares the e4 advance that completes White's pawn centre. White is playing for the space this structure gives, and Black must find counterplay on the queenside.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 d6 5.e4.strategy: Builds the full pawn centre at once, with the e4 pawn backing the one on d5. White gets maximum space and plays in the centre and on the kingside, but the pieces still have to catch up, and the advanced pawns need constant support against Black's queenside majority.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 d6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and prepares to castle, leaving the centre pawns where they are. White keeps the choice of set-up open and waits for Black to show a plan, at the cost of delaying the full pawn centre the structure offers.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 exd5 4.cxd5 d6 5.Nc.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which will press the long diagonal against White's centre. Black does not contest the centre directly: it lets White build it and plans to undermine it from the side and from a distance.

Attacks d5 and controls e4, the natural developing move. Sound, but White builds a broad centre and can add a kingside pawn advance, while Black must keep the weak d6 pawn safe and make the queenside play count before White's attack arrives.

Prepares to expand on the queenside with ...b5 and takes the b5 square away from White's pieces. It is slow, though: it spends a tempo while White develops, and White can stop the plan altogether. Playable, but it commits a pawn before the pieces are out.

Completes the pawn centre, with pawns on d5 and e4 and the knight behind them. White gains the space the structure promises and aims for the centre and kingside, but the advanced pawns must be kept supported.

Develops the kingside knight and prepares to castle, leaving the centre pawns where they are. White waits to see where Black puts the pieces and can still take the centre later, but gives Black time to complete the fianchetto and start pressing on the long diagonal.

Quiet and positional: the bishop on g2 will back the d5 pawn from a distance, and White does not build the pawn centre. Sound, but it passes up much of the space advantage the structure offers, so Black's counterplay on the queenside comes more easily.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop presses on the long diagonal, on the knight on c3 and on the centre, and the king's bishop is developed. Black leaves White the centre on purpose and plans to undermine it with the queenside majority.

Hits e4 so White must keep it supported, but a further pawn advance, f4, builds a broad centre with a kingside attack to follow. Sound, but Black is under pressure before its pieces and its queenside play are ready.

Prepares to expand on the queenside and denies White the b5 square, but spends a tempo while White's pawn centre is complete and White has a free hand. Playable, but it leaves Black behind in development.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4.strategy: Trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and removes the tension in the centre. White recaptures with a developing move, but Black's position is solid and free of weaknesses.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Challenges the c4 pawn at once and heads for a Tarrasch-type structure: after the exchanges Black gets free piece play, but accepts an isolated pawn on d5 or hanging pawns that White can aim at. An active choice that trades structure for activity.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and controls e4 and d5, leaving the tension in the centre for later. Black can still trade on d4, and if White pushes the d-pawn, Black trades and plays for a queenside majority against White's central one. A flexible, safe move.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Recaptures with a developing move and centralises the knight, where it eyes e6, c6 and b5. White keeps the c-pawn as a space edge on the queenside, and Black has to deal with the active knight.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which centralises it but exposes it: ...Nc6 attacks the queen with a developing move, and White must spend another tempo retreating it. Sound, but Black gains time and is the first to develop a second piece.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.e3.strategy: Gambits the pawn instead of recapturing: after ...dxe3 the bishop retakes and White has some lead in development, but Black has no weaknesses and an extra pawn. Not enough compensation for a pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Anti-Benoni Variation, Spielmann Defence
1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it controls e4 and d5. That brakes White's attempt to build a broad centre with e4 and prepares quick castling. Black accepts a little less space for a solid, easy game.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the knight and puts a piece in the centre at once, challenging White's most active piece. If White exchanges, Black recaptures with the b-pawn, gaining a half-open b-file but leaving the a-pawn isolated. An active, sound plan that accepts a loosened queenside structure.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6.strategy: A waiting move that takes the b5 square from White's pieces and prepares a compact, flexible set-up with the queen on c7. It spends a tempo, so White can take space in the centre, and Black keeps a sound but slightly cramped game.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: the knight guards e5 and d4, prepares castling and leaves the choice of set-up open. White commits nothing in the centre, so Black has to show which kind of Dutch it wants while White keeps a quiet, solid edge in development.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nc3.name: Dutch Defence: Rubinstein Variation
1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to its most active square, adding pressure on e4 and d5 and leaving White the choice between a fianchetto and a classical set-up. The price is that Black can pin the knight at once with the bishop, so White has to be ready to unpin.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.e4.name: Dutch Defence: Bellon Gambit
1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.e4.strategy: Offers a pawn to blow open the centre against the weakened kingside, but Black simply takes it and develops. White has to prove that quick development and open lines are worth the pawn, and against calm play they are not.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight guards e4 and h5, covering the diagonal that the f-pawn advance has weakened, and prepares castling. Black keeps all its set-ups open and fights for the centre from the flank instead of occupying it.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a safe square and prepares castling, while Black's pawn structure stays undecided. The bishop does not block the knight's best square, and Black can still choose between a closed wall of pawns and a more elastic set-up once White shows its plan.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Bb4+.strategy: Gives check to disturb White's development, and if the knight blocks, Black can take it and double White's pawns. But the bishop has little else to aim at, and a trade on d2 gives up the dark-squared bishop that would guard the kingside weakened by the f-pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: White's usual plan against the Dutch: the bishop will rule the long diagonal and the e4 square that Black's f-pawn fights for, while the king gets a safe home. It trades immediate action for a slow, positional game in which White probes the weakened kingside.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Puts the queen's knight on its natural square, where it eyes e4 and d5 and keeps the choice between a fianchetto and a classical set-up with e3 and Be2. It is flexible but less pointed than the fianchetto, and it leaves the c-pawn's file blocked.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6 knight against the queen and aims to trade it, since that knight guards e4 and h5 and so holds back White's central advance. It brings the bishop out before e3 shuts it in, but Black can break the pin or recapture easily, so White gains little.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6.strategy: Starts the Stonewall: with ...d5 to follow, the pawns on f5, e6, d5 and c6 form a wall that grips e4. Black gains a solid, static structure and a secure king, but locks in the light-squared bishop and hands White the e5 square as an outpost.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7.strategy: Develops the king's bishop on its most solid square and prepares castling, while the d-pawn stays flexible. Black keeps the choice between locking the centre behind a wall of pawns and a more elastic structure, and keeps the king safe for the kingside play the f-pawn is meant to start.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Takes a firm grip on e4 and the light squares at once, building the wall of pawns on f5, e6 and d5. It commits the d-pawn before the pieces are developed and shuts in the light-squared bishop, and White can release the tension in the centre with cxd5.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 d6.strategy: Keeps the e6 pawn solid and supports a later central break with the e-pawn. This is the older, more elastic set-up and a sound one, but it leaves e4 less firmly held than a pawn on d5 does, so Black is slower to take control of the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop is hemmed in by its own knight for now, but it aims along the long diagonal at e4 and the centre Black is building, and gains force when the knight moves or the centre is opened.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight to its natural square and adds pressure on d5 and e4 before Black has built the wall. It commits the knight to a square where it blocks the c-pawn, so the fight against the closed structure is slower than with the fianchetto.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.b3.strategy: Prepares to trade Black's dark-squared bishop by bringing a bishop to a3, removing the piece that would guard e5 and the kingside dark squares. It also readies the queen's bishop for the long diagonal, but it weakens c3 and delays the king's bishop.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the Stonewall wall and takes a firm grip of e4, the square the f-pawn is meant to control. Black commits to a closed, solid structure with a kingside attacking plan, accepting a passive light-squared bishop and a weak e5 square.

Develops the bishop on the safe square and prepares castling, keeping the d-pawn undecided. The bishop does little beyond guarding the kingside, so Black plays for a solid, slightly passive position and relies on the structure rather than activity.

Takes e5 with a pawn instead of a piece and keeps the e6 pawn protected, aiming for a later central break with the e-pawn. It gives up the firm grip on e4 that a pawn on d5 provides, so White can play in the centre more freely.

Brings the king to safety behind the fianchetto and connects the rooks. White keeps its plans flexible: the e5 outpost, a trade of Black's good bishop and a later central break are all still available against the closed Stonewall structure.

Develops the queen's knight at once and adds pressure on d5 and e4, leaving castling for later. White plays for the e5 outpost and the trade of Black's dark-squared bishop, but the king stays in the centre a move longer.

Prepares Ba3 to offer a trade of Black's dark-squared bishop, the piece that guards e5 and the kingside, or Bb2 on the long diagonal. It delays castling, so Black gets time to settle the structure and White needs more than this to cause problems.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.name: Dutch Defence: Stonewall Variation, Modern Variation
1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.background: Interest in the Stonewall revived in the 1980s and 1990s, when Artur Yusupov, Sergey Dolmatov, Nigel Short and Simen Agdestein helped develop this version, with ...d5 played early and the dark-squared bishop on d6. It has stayed more popular than the traditional set-up with the bishop on e7.
1.d4 e6 2.c4 f5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the diagonal that contests e5, the outpost White's knight wants, and aims it at the kingside. This is the more active way to set up the Stonewall, because the dark-squared bishop gets a real job before Black castles and plays for a kingside attack.

Develops the bishop to a solid square and prepares castling. The bishop guards the kingside but does not contest e5, so Black accepts a slightly passive set-up and relies on the wall of pawns to keep the position closed and safe.

Plants the knight on the outpost that the f5 and d5 pawns support, cramping White and preparing to play on the kingside. White can trade it off or undermine its supports, and until the dark-squared bishop is developed Black's pieces are still unco-ordinated.
